title: Flood Fill
problemStatement: You are given an image (2D grid of integers representing colors), a starting pixel (sr, sc), and a newColor. Perform a flood fill: starting from the pixel, change its color and the color of every pixel connected to it (4-directionally) that has the SAME original color, to newColor.
approachSteps: This is exactly graph connectivity, where each grid cell is a node connected to its up/down/left/right neighbors of the same color.
Remember the starting pixel's original color before you change anything (otherwise your 'same color' check breaks after the first change).
If the new color equals the original color, do nothing — otherwise, naive recursion could infinite-loop revisiting already-filled cells.
DFS (or BFS) from the start: if the current cell matches the original color, set it to newColor, then recurse into its 4 neighbors that are within bounds.
Each cell is only ever processed once because once its color is changed to newColor, it no longer matches the 'original color' check.

bruteForce.approach: There isn't a meaningfully different brute force here — DFS/BFS is already the natural and optimal approach for connectivity problems.

optimalApproach: DFS (or BFS) from the start pixel, recoloring same-colored connected pixels and recursing into in-bounds neighbors; the color check itself prevents revisiting.
solutionCode:
def flood_fill(image, sr, sc, new_color):
    original = image[sr][sc]
    if original == new_color:
        return image

    rows, cols = len(image), len(image[0])

    def dfs(r, c):
        if r < 0 or r >= rows or c < 0 or c >= cols or image[r][c] != original:
            return
        image[r][c] = new_color
        dfs(r + 1, c)
        dfs(r - 1, c)
        dfs(r, c + 1)
        dfs(r, c - 1)

    dfs(sr, sc)
    return image
timeComplexity: O(rows * cols) — each cell is visited and recolored at most once.
spaceComplexity: O(rows * cols) worst case for the recursion stack (e.g. a grid that's a single connected snake).
followUps: Why is checking original == new_color upfront necessary for correctness, not just an optimization?
How would you rewrite this iteratively with an explicit stack or queue to avoid recursion depth limits on large grids?

title: Number of Islands
problemStatement: Given an m x n 2D binary grid grid which represents a map of '1's (land) and '0's (water), return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.
approachSteps: An 'island' is a connected component of land cells — this is graph connectivity again, but now you need to COUNT distinct components, not just fill one.
Scan every cell in the grid in order.
Whenever you find an unvisited land cell ('1'), that's the start of a NEW island — increment the island count.
Immediately DFS (or BFS) from that cell, marking every connected land cell as visited (e.g. by flipping it to '0' or using a separate visited set) so it's never counted again.
Continue the outer scan; because visited land is marked, each island is only ever discovered and counted once, no matter its shape or size.

bruteForce.approach: There isn't a fundamentally different brute force — scanning + connected-component marking is already optimal; the only variation is DFS vs BFS vs Union-Find.

optimalApproach: Scan every cell; on an unvisited land cell, increment the island count and flood-fill (DFS/BFS) to mark the whole connected component as visited so it's not recounted.
timeComplexity: O(rows * cols) — every cell is visited a constant number of times total (once by the outer scan, plus once when flood-filled).
spaceComplexity: O(rows * cols) worst case for the DFS recursion stack (a grid that's entirely one island).
followUps: How would you solve this with Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) instead of DFS, and when might that be preferable?
How would 'Number of Islands II' (islands added one at a time, count after each addition) change your approach?

title: Course Schedule
problemStatement: There are numCourses courses labeled 0 to numCourses-1. You are given prerequisites where prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means you must take course b before course a. Return true if you can finish all courses (i.e., there is no cycle in the prerequisite graph), false otherwise.

examples.explanation: Course 0 needs course 1 and vice versa — a cycle, impossible.

approachSteps: 'Can all courses be finished' is exactly asking: is this directed graph of prerequisites acyclic? A valid course order is a topological sort, which only exists for a DAG (no cycles).
Build an adjacency list and compute each course's in-degree (number of prerequisites it still needs).
Start a queue with every course that has in-degree 0 (no prerequisites — can be taken immediately).
Repeatedly pop a course from the queue, 'take' it, and decrement the in-degree of every course that depends on it — if any of those drops to 0, push it onto the queue.

Count how many courses were successfully taken this way. If it equals numCourses, every course was reachable in valid order (no cycle); if fewer, some courses are stuck in a cycle and were never freed up.

bruteForce.approach: DFS from each node tracking the current recursion path (a 'visiting' set); if you ever revisit a node that's still in the current path, that's a cycle.

optimalApproach: Kahn's algorithm: BFS topological sort using in-degrees. If the number of courses processed equals numCourses, the graph is acyclic and completion is possible.
solutionCode:
from collections import deque, defaultdict

def can_finish(num_courses, prerequisites):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    in_degree = [0] * num_courses

    for course, prereq in prerequisites:
        graph[prereq].append(course)
        in_degree[course] += 1

    queue = deque([c for c in range(num_courses) if in_degree[c] == 0])
    taken = 0

    while queue:
        course = queue.popleft()
        taken += 1
        for next_course in graph[course]:
            in_degree[next_course] -= 1
            if in_degree[next_course] == 0:
                queue.append(next_course)

    return taken == num_courses
timeComplexity: O(V + E) — V courses and E prerequisite edges, each processed a constant number of times.
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) for the adjacency list, in-degree array, and queue.
followUps: How would you modify this to return a valid course ORDER, not just true/false (Course Schedule II)?
Walk through the DFS 'visiting/visited' cycle-detection alternative — why does a two-color (or three-color) marking scheme matter there?
